item.vignette: A 7-year-old boy has progressively slowed linear growth and proportionate short stature. Evaluation establishes isolated growth hormone deficiency. Sequencing identifies a biallelic variant in a receptor gene. In a research assay using otherwise identical cells, the normal receptor binds growth hormone-releasing hormone, but the patient-derived receptor does not. The hormone preparation activates cells expressing the normal receptor.
item.lead_in: Which normal endocrine interaction is directly disrupted by this receptor defect?

options.A: Growth hormone acting on receptors in hepatocytes
options.B: IGF-1 acting on receptors in growth-plate cells
options.C: Growth hormone-releasing hormone acting on pituitary somatotrophs
options.D: Somatostatin acting on receptors in pituitary somatotrophs
options.E: Thyroid-stimulating hormone acting on thyroid follicular cells

item.tested_construct: Localize GHRHR loss to hypothalamic GHRH recognition by pituitary somatotrophs, distinguishing releasing-hormone resistance from peripheral GH resistance.
item.difficulty_basis: Expert estimate; not psychometrically calibrated. Requires applying the stated phenotype or functional experiment to a specific endocrine defect.

option_rationales.A: Hepatic GH responsiveness is downstream of GH secretion; it is not the receptor-ligand pair tested in the assay.
option_rationales.B: IGF-1 responsiveness is downstream of the stated releasing-hormone receptor defect.
option_rationales.C: GHRHR on somatotrophs recognizes GHRH and promotes GH synthesis and release. Failure to bind GHRH disrupts this interaction.
option_rationales.D: This is a different ligand-receptor interaction; the assay specifically tests GHRH recognition.
option_rationales.E: This is a different pituitary-target axis and does not account for the demonstrated GHRH-binding defect.

explanation.educational_objective: Distinguish failure of pituitary GHRH reception from defects in downstream GH action.

item.vignette: A 3-week-old boy has recurrent episodes of lethargy with laboratory-confirmed hypoglycemia. Insulin secretion remains inappropriately high during these episodes. Genetic testing identifies biallelic loss-of-function variants in ABCC8. Functional studies show markedly reduced activity of the channel containing the encoded protein.
item.lead_in: Which change most directly links this defect to inappropriate insulin secretion?

options.A: Reduced activity of beta-cell ATP-sensitive potassium channels
options.B: Reduced phosphorylation of glucose by beta-cell glucokinase
options.C: Persistent opening of beta-cell ATP-sensitive potassium channels
options.D: Reduced binding of insulin to receptors on skeletal muscle cells
options.E: Reduced sensitivity of beta cells to a rise in glucose concentration

item.tested_construct: ABCC8-associated loss of KATP channel function and inappropriate beta-cell insulin secretion.
item.difficulty_basis: Expert estimate; not psychometrically calibrated. Requires applying the stated phenotype or functional experiment to a specific endocrine defect.

option_rationales.A: ABCC8 encodes a KATP-channel subunit. Loss of channel function can produce insulin excess despite low glucose.
option_rationales.B: Reduced glucokinase activity impairs glucose sensing and favors hyperglycemia rather than this channel defect.
option_rationales.C: Channels that remain open impair insulin release and are associated with neonatal diabetes.
option_rationales.D: This concerns peripheral insulin action, whereas the supplied genetic and functional evidence localizes the defect to a beta-cell channel.
option_rationales.E: Reduced glucose sensing is the opposite direction from secretion persisting during hypoglycemia and does not identify the defective channel.

explanation.educational_objective: Connect loss of beta-cell KATP-channel function to inappropriate insulin release, and distinguish it from channels that fail to close.

item.vignette: A 19-year-old woman has mildly elevated fasting glucose documented since childhood, without progressive symptoms. Her father has a similar pattern. Testing identifies a heterozygous loss-of-function variant in GCK. A research team studies glucose-stimulated insulin release from beta cells carrying this variant.
item.lead_in: Which abnormality is most directly attributable to the function of the affected protein?

options.A: Reduced transcription of genes regulating beta-cell development
options.B: Failure of a potassium-channel subunit to respond to rising ATP
options.C: Reduced insulin responsiveness of peripheral target tissues
options.D: Accelerated immune-mediated loss of pancreatic beta cells
options.E: Impaired detection of increasing glucose concentrations by beta cells

item.tested_construct: Distinguish glucokinase glucose sensing from transcription-factor, ion-channel and peripheral-action defects in monogenic hyperglycemia.
item.difficulty_basis: Expert estimate; not psychometrically calibrated. Requires applying the stated phenotype or functional experiment to a specific endocrine defect.

option_rationales.A: HNF-family MODY proteins regulate transcription; glucokinase instead participates in glucose sensing.
option_rationales.B: This describes a channel defect rather than the function of glucokinase.
option_rationales.C: The specified lesion affects glucose sensing in beta cells; the question does not identify a peripheral insulin-receptor lesion.
option_rationales.D: The supplied causal finding is a glucose-sensing enzyme defect, not immune destruction.
option_rationales.E: Reduced glucokinase function impairs the beta-cell response to rising glucose, explaining persistent mild hyperglycemia.

explanation.educational_objective: Identify impaired glucose sensing as the beta-cell consequence of GCK loss of function.

item.vignette: A 15-year-old girl has severe obesity and persistent hunger beginning in infancy. In a research study, her circulating leptin activates a normal leptin-receptor reporter system. Cells engineered to express her receptor have normal receptor abundance at the surface and normal leptin binding, but little intracellular signaling after leptin exposure. Otherwise identical cells expressing the normal receptor signal appropriately.
item.lead_in: Which defect best explains these results?

options.A: Reduced synthesis of leptin in adipocytes
options.B: Impaired coupling of the leptin receptor to intracellular signaling
options.C: Reduced affinity of the leptin receptor for its ligand
options.D: Accelerated removal of leptin from the circulation
options.E: Impaired secretion of leptin from adipocytes

item.tested_construct: Use ligand activity, surface abundance, binding and matched-cell controls to localize leptin resistance to receptor signal transduction.
item.difficulty_basis: Expert estimate; not psychometrically calibrated. Requires applying the stated phenotype or functional experiment to a specific endocrine defect.

option_rationales.A: Ligand production cannot explain failed signaling in cells exposed to the same active leptin preparation.
option_rationales.B: Normal binding with impaired downstream signaling localizes the functional defect beyond ligand recognition.
option_rationales.C: Ligand binding is explicitly preserved in the assay.
option_rationales.D: Circulatory clearance does not explain different responses under matched cell-culture exposure.
option_rationales.E: A secretion defect cannot explain failure of receptor-bearing cells given an active ligand directly.

explanation.educational_objective: Distinguish defective leptin-receptor signal transmission from deficient ligand production, delivery or binding.

item.vignette: A 24-year-old woman is evaluated for infertility. She had normal breast and pubic-hair development but has had infrequent menstrual periods since late adolescence. Evaluation shows anovulation. Her 46,XY sibling has female external genitalia, undescended testes, and markedly underdeveloped Leydig cells. Sequencing finds the same biallelic loss-of-function receptor variant in both siblings.
item.lead_in: Failure to respond to which pair of hormones most directly explains the shared receptor defect?

options.D: Luteinizing hormone and human chorionic gonadotropin
options.E: Growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor 1

item.tested_construct: Identify the shared LH/hCG receptor from female anovulation and male Leydig-cell hypoplasia in siblings.
item.difficulty_basis: Expert estimate; not psychometrically calibrated. Requires applying the stated phenotype or functional experiment to a specific endocrine defect.

option_rationales.A: Androgens share the androgen receptor, but impaired androgen action does not explain the stated Leydig-cell underdevelopment as directly as impaired LH/hCG reception.
option_rationales.B: These act through different receptors; they are not the two ligands of the receptor controlling Leydig-cell development and function.
option_rationales.C: These use distinct steroid receptors and do not identify the shared Leydig-cell receptor.
option_rationales.D: LH and hCG bind LHCGR. Loss impairs Leydig-cell development/testosterone production and can cause anovulation in 46,XX individuals.
option_rationales.E: These act at different steps of the growth axis, not as two ligands of the gonadal receptor.

explanation.educational_objective: Connect the two ligands of LHCGR to sex-specific consequences of loss of receptor function.
